stem: A55-year-old woman who had rheumatic fever at the age of 13 is admitted to the Emergency Department with palpitations and exertional dyspnoea. Over the past two months, she has suffered a progressive fall in her exercise tolerance, such that she is no longer able to run for the bus. Her blood pressure is 137/82 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There is a pan-systolic murmur which is loudest at the apex. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The murmur here is consistent with mitral regurgitation related to rheumatic fever, where initial symptoms may occur very late, because of significant systolic dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension or the onset of atrial fibrillation. Q.

stem: A72-year-old retired gardener presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 1cm ulcerated lesion on his right temple with a rolled edge. He tells you that it has grown slowly over the past six months. He has had previous basal- and squamous-cell carcinomas removed over the past five years. You note a number of telangiectasia around the margins of the lesion and superficial ulceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: With a large ulcerated basal-cell carcinoma(BCC) lesion on the temple, topical therapies, cryotherapy or photodynamic therapy are unlikely to be effective. A 4 mm excision margin is recommended, although where this is difficult to attain on the head and neck, micrographic surgical techniques may be considered. Q.

stem: A19-year-old man with atopic eczema comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has developed a fever over the past 36 hours and now has a worsening of his erythema with multiple pustules and vesicles which are intensely itchy. He has recently been using a higher potency steroid cream for the eczema. His temperature is 38.9℃, blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg,and his pulse is 90 bpm and regular. The vesicles are spread over his neck, torso and upper arms. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The suspicion here is of eczema herpeticum, which is related to herpes simplex virus 1(HSV1) infection in patients with existing atopic eczema. Left untreated, it may progress to disseminated HSV infection, leading to death. IV aciclovir is therefore the intervention of choice. Q.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review with his partner. He has previously had difficulty forming relationships and reports difficulty now with his sex drive and maintaining his erections during sexual intercourse. Examination reveals evidence of gynaecomastia, sparse pubic and axillary hair and small testes. Blood pressure is normal at 122/82mmHg, his BMl is normal at 23 kg/mand his weight is stable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his sexual dysfunction?
explanation: The picture of longstanding sexual dysfunction with small testes and gynaecomastia, fits well with a diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome with XXY haplotype. Testosterone replacement is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He has suffered from multiple joint pains over the past six months, coupled with gradual weight loss and intermittent diarrhoea and bloating. He also tells you that his stool floats and is difficult to flush away. He also has a chronic cough for which his GP has prescribed a salbutamol inhaler with no significant improvement and has noticed increased skin tanning. Examination reveals increased skin pigmentation and a reduced body mass index(BMI) of 20 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The triad seen here of chronic cough, weight loss with steatorrhoea and arthritis is consistent with a diagnosis of Whipple's. Small-bowel biopsy, which is diagnostic for the condition, is likely to show infiltration of the lamina propria with Periodic acid-Schiff(PAS)-positive macrophages. Up to one to two years of antibiotic therapy may be required to clear the responsible organism, Tropheryma whipplei. It is a rare example of a disease where co-trimoxazole may be used for a long period. Q.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) comes to the clinic for review. Her disease is well controlled and she came off medication three months ago to try and get pregnant. She is worried about risk of venous thromboembolism in pregnancy. Which of the following antibodies is most associated with risk of venous thromboembolism?
explanation: Anti-phospholipid antibodies, which lead to prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time(APTT), increase risk of venous thromboembolism and early pregnancy loss due to impairment of placental function. Aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin,in the context of SLE, has been shown to reduce the risk of spontaneous miscarriage. Q.

stem: A54-year-old taxi driver is referred to the Respiratory Clinic having momentarily lost concentration, causing a road accident. His wife reports him to be a heavy snorer, who stops breathing on occasions during the night. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. Examination reveals quiet wheeze on auscultation, his body mass index is 35 kg/m. Which of the following investigations would lead to a diagnosis?
explanation: The history here and findings on examination fit best with a diagnosis of sleep apnoea. Polysomnography records not only oximetry, but also pulse, blood pressure and evidence of awakenings. This gives a much more robust answer as to the burden of sleep apnoea than oximetry alone. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is currently taking the combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP) and is sexually active but is concerned,as she often forgets to take it. She has no plans of starting a family in near future. What is the most appropriate alternative contraception for her?
explanation: Copper intrauterine device (IUD) is correct. Intrauterine devices are a good choice for adolescent and adult women who:1- Desire one highly effective contraceptive method.2- Desire long-term yet reversible contraception. 3-Want or need to avoid estrogen exposure (all IUDs) or progestin exposure (copper IUDs) Q.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has reported intermittent regurgitation of solid food for up to two years and has lost up to 3 kg in weight during that time. Apart from intermittent symptoms of reflux and hypertension, he is otherwise well. Physical examination is unremarkable, and a barium swallow has shown a bird's beak appearance typical for achalasia. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for his oesophageal dysfunction?
options: Disordered motility of the upper third of the oesophagus
Failure of relaxation of the cardiac sphincter
explanation: There are a number of reasons which are thought to drive development of achalasia, the underlying diagnosis here. These include failure of the cardiac or lower oesophageal sphincter to relax adequately, and disordered motility in the lower third of the oesophagus. Treatment can include calcium-channel blockers, nitrates, and injection of botulinum toxin into the sphincter. Q.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has recently been diagnosed with primary pulmonary hypertension(PPH) and asks about prognosis. Which of the following is most associated with poor prognosis in PPH?
options: Elevated N-terminal (NT) pro B-type natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP)
explanation: Elevated NT pro-BNP is a signal of right ventricular dysfunction, which is associated with poor prognosis in patients with PPH. Other indicators of poor right ventricular function include reduced right ventricular ejection fraction and supraventricular arrhythmias.

stem: A74-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with severe retrosternal chest pain after eating a steak meal. He tells you that he had a sensation of a piece of steak being stuck that persisted until just after he arrived in the Emergency Department. On further questioning, it transpires he has suffered from symptoms of reflux with solid food intermittently sticking and has lost 6 kg in weight over the past six weeks without trying. His body mass index(BMI) is 22 kg/m and he is tender in the epigastrium. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 99 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Normal.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has primary pulmonary hypertension(PPH) and has recently commenced therapy with bosentan. Her blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular and her chest is clear. She has a 2-year-old son and would like to know about her prognosis. Which of the following would be an indicator of poor prognosis for this patient?
options: Increased right ventricular compliance on echocardiogram
explanation: Development of AF implies worsening pulmonary hypertension and atrial dilatation. Development of AF is therefore a poor prognostic indicator in primary pulmonary hypertension. Difficulty.

stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She wishes to commence the oral contraceptive pill but wants to discuss the impact it may have on her risk of cancer. Which of the following cancers is most increased in patients who take the combined oral contraceptive pill?
explanation: Taking the oral contraceptive pill (OCP) for five years or more doubles the risk of cervical cancer for a woman versus one who has never taken the pill. The risk falls back once the pill is discontinued, and by the time ten years have passed since the pillis stopped, the risk of cervical cancer is the same as that for a woman who has never taken it. Difficulty.

stem: A 61-year-old man who has type 2 diabetes currently managed with gliclazide 80 mg two times a day, is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered a hypo after drinking a number of pints of beer at a wedding. His usual glycosylated haemoglobin(HbA1c) is 55 mmol/mol and he hasn't suffered a hypoglycaemic episode before. His body mass index is elevated at 31 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely primary cause of his hypoglycaemic episode?
explanation: Studies in animals suggest that alcohol impacts on the pancreatic microcirculation leading to increased beta- cell perfusion and over-shoot of the first-phase insulin response. This is thought to be responsible for the increased risk of hypoglycaemia in patients with type 2 diabetes who drink alcohol. Difficulty.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has suffered from slowly progressive heart failure and atrial fibrillation, and over the past five to ten years, has developed gradually worsening proximal muscle weakness. Examination in the clinic confirms proximal muscle weakness and mild pitting oedema affecting both ankles. Which of the following pathologies is known to underlie the progressive muscular weakness seen here?
explanation: Telomere shortening in muscle stem cells is thought to underpin the progressive muscular weakness seen in both Duchenne's and Becker's muscular dystrophy(Becker's is the most likely diagnosis here). Telomere shortening is thought to drive a loss in ability to regenerate new muscle. Difficulty.

stem: A 29-year-old man is left at the front door of the Emergency Department. He has received a stab wound to his left upper chest. His blood pressure is 89/70 mmHg, pulse is 138 bpm and regular. O saturations are 90% on 10 litres of O.There are no breath sounds on auscultation of the left side of the chest. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cannula insertion into the second intercostal space midclavicular line
explanation: This patient has a tension pneumothorax and urgent intervention is required. There is significant risk of cardiorespiratory arrest. In this situation, insertion of a cannula is essential, there is no time to waste waiting for radiology or formal chest drain insertion. Difficuty.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Immunology Clinic with recurrent sinusitis, lower respiratory tract infections and bronchiectasis. He has had four hospital stays because of lower respiratory tract infection over the past year. He tells you that he has always been sickly and has suffered from respiratory tract infections every year for as long as he can remember. On auscultation, you can hear crackles at both lung bases consistent with bronchiectasis. Which of the following is he most likely to be suffering from?
explanation: Most patients with IgG1 deficiency also have hypogammaglobulinaemia because lgG1 makes up around two thirds of total IgG.Around 80% of patients with IgG1 deficiency suffer from recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and around 20% of the total have asthma. Vaccination is essential, and prophylactic antibiotics may be considered for some patients with recurrent infection. Difficulty.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has suffered from multiple joint pains affecting her hands, wrists, elbows, knees and feet over the past 12 weeks. Symptoms have failed to respond to regular naproxen. Examination reveals evidence of small-joint polyarthritis, with metacarpophalangeal joint(MCP) joint inflammation. Which of the following is the best initial investigation for detecting early rheumatoid joint changes in the hands?
explanation: Ultrasound is non-invasive and easier to obtain than MRI scanning in many centres and can identify synovial inflammation in MCP joints at an earlier stage than plain radiography. As such, it makes it an obvious initial investigation in rheumatoid arthritis. Difficulty.

stem: You are called by the Cardiac Arrest Team to a 54-year-old man who has suffered a cardiac arrest and is in pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). He is just completing the fifth cycle of defibrillation and has received amiodarone 300 mg after the third cycle. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step apart from continuing cycles of cardiopulmonary resuscitation(CPR) with adrenalin and defibrillation?
explanation: Adult life support(ALS) guidelines recommend a further dose of 150 mg amiodarone in patients who remain in pulseless VT despite five cycles of CPR and an initial 300 mg bolus of amiodarone after the third shock. Difficulty.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the midwife some five days after the birth of her first child. She is tearful, tired, and lacks confidence that she is able to look after her baby,feeling that no matter what she does it isn't good enough. She has not expressed any thoughts of harming herself or her child. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Postpartum blues with mild symptoms of depression usually develop between five and ten days postpartum. In this case, with no symptoms of major depression and no thoughts of self-harming or harming the child, increased support and surveillance is adequate. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines recommend self-help strategies, non-directed counselling and/or a brief psychological treatment. Q. stem: A 22-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic following the sudden death of his father, while playing squash at the age of 48.He is well and has no significant symptoms of cardiac disease. Examination in the clinic reveals a blood pressure of 148/84 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 24kg/m.He has no cardiac murmurs and his chest is clear. Electrocardiogram(ECG) reveals evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiogram(ECHO) reveals evidence of asymmetrical septal hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance for his cardiovascular condition?
explanation: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy(HOCM), the underlying diagnosis here, is inherited in an autosomal-dominant fashion. Across all study populations, mutations in the cardiac myosin-binding protein-.

She had an episode of renal stones one year earlier, had a Colles'fracture some nine months ago, and feels tired, but has no other specific symptoms. Her blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg,pulse is 63 bpm and regular, body mass index(BMI) is 24 kg/m. He has recently returned from Pakistan where he was staying with his uncle who has just been diagnosed with active tuberculosis(TB). He has no respiratory symptoms and clinical examination is unremarkable. What is the best way to confirm that he has infectious TB?

stem: A 21-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with symptomatic hypoglycaemia, nausea, vomiting and dehydration. She has low blood pressure of 85/60 mmHg and looks tanned. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 128 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the main cause of this patient's increased skin pigmentation?
explanation: This patient has autoimmune adrenal failure, leading to the nausea, vomiting,hypotension, hyperkalaemia.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe epigastric pain, vomiting and hyperventilation. He drinks five units of alcohol per week. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 102 bpm and regular. He is very tender in the epigastrium. Body mass index(BMI) is 22 kg/m.Bloods confirm elevated amylase and lipase consistent with pancreatitis, the sample is reported as lipaemic, so no cholesterol results are reported. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his pancreatitis?
explanation: Given this patient's age, body habitus and lack of alcohol consumption, dyslipidaemia, in this case FH,is the.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has left hip pain which is significantly limiting his walking, and his GP has noted abnormal liver function tests. Examination reveals significant limitation of flexion and external rotation of the left hip. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation? stem: A42-year-old climber has recently returned from a trip to the Himalayas. Which of the following is likely to be found on routine assessment in the sports medicine clinic?
explanation: Chronic hypoxia associated with high altitude leads to compensatory changes to improve oxygen delivery to tissues. One such compensatory change is increased production of Hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha(HIF1- alpha), which drives increased production of red blood cells.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is treated with vincristine for leukaemia. She has developed neuropathic pain. Which of the following describes the stage of the cell cycle that vincristine acts on?
explanation: Vincristine is an antineoplastic drug with broad-spectrum anti-tumour activity. Indications include a range of haematological malignancies, neuroblastoma and rhabdomyosarcoma. The drug is thought to act by mitotic inhibition, causing an arrest of cell division in metaphase by interfering with microtubule polymerisation.A number of oncology drugs act during the metaphase because this is the point in mitosis when chromosomes are duplicated.

stem: You are called as part of the arrest team to see a 57-year-old man who is receiving the first unit of a blood transfusion, having undergone nailing of a fractured femur. He sustained the injury in a road traffic collision. He has become extremely unwell after receiving only around 10 ml of the unit of blood. He is flushed with rigors and shortness of breath, complaining of pain in his abdomen and at the site of the transfusion cannula. His temperature is 38.0℃, pulse is 110 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has suffered a rapid deterioration in his condition after only a few ml of blood transfusion.A rapidly progressive reaction occurs when the patient's own anti-A or anti-B antibodies react with the transfused red blood cells. This can also promote complement activation, significantly accelerating any deterioration in pulse and blood pressure.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who has become pregnant against medical advice comes to the Emergency Department with a three day history of palpitations. She is 24 weeks'pregnant and has mitral stenosis. Her blood pressure is 105/82 mmHg, pulse is 130 bpm (atrial fibrillation). Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The main risk of mitral stenosis in pregnancy is the development of decompensated heart failure with rate uncontrolled atrial fibrillation. In this case, beta-blockade with an agent such as bisoprolol should be instigated to slow the ventricular rate. The concerns about beta-blockade and intra-uterine growth retardation are most when the agents are prescribed in the first trimester.

stem: A 56-year-old man is about to undergo a left nephrectomy for an underlying renal carcinoma. With respect to anatomy, what structure may overlie the left renal hilum?
explanation: The tail of the pancreas may extend to overlie the hilum of the left kidney.

stem: A 19-year-old is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered a brief fainting episode whilst at the dentist. Immediately post a dental extraction, he lost consciousness whilst sitting in the dentist's chair. There was a brief episode of limb jerking and head shaking which resolved when he was laid flat. He recovered consciousness after 40 seconds with no postictal phenomena. Neurological examination is unremarkable, as are routine bloods. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This history with a head-up faint, almost certainly the cause of the limb jerking seen here,is consistent with vasovagal syncope. This is no doubt related to the dental extraction.No further investigation is indicated; this patient can be reassured and discharged.

stem: A42-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and takes hydroxychloroquine has well- controlled joint disease but is beginning to suffer from dry eyes and dry mucus membranes. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be associated with this patient's new symptoms?
explanation: Anti-Ro antibodies, along with anti-La antibodies, are found with increased frequency in patients with Sjogren's, which is responsible for the symptoms here. Sjogren's itself is more likely to occur against a background of SLE.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. Over the past few months, he has developed intermittent night sweats, gradual weight loss, and arthralgia affecting his back and knees. He is most concerned, as he has developed ulcers affecting his mouth and tongue and his penis. He has also developed red, itchy eyes. Examination reveals evidence of uveitis, arthritis affecting the lower back and knees, and aphthous ulcers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: This patient has a presentation consistent with Bechet syndrome, including non-specific symptoms of vasculitis, and the triad of uveitis, oral and genital ulceration. Prednisolone is the initial intervention of choice for systemic symptoms, with azathioprine added as a second-line steroid-sparing agent; one to two years or more of therapy may be required.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who has recently diagnosed hypertension and type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review.She has also had difficulties with swelling of the fingers of both hands and has noticed a change in the shape of her lower jaw on photographs taken over the past two to three years. An insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) sent by her GP is markedly elevated. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 72 bpm and regular. Her body mass index(BMI) is 24 kg/m. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Glucose tolerance test with growth-hormone(GH) measurement
explanation: This patient has acromegaly and the best way to confirm the diagnosis is with an oral glucose tolerance test. GH is normally inhibited by glucose. If the glucose load fails to suppress the GH below 1.0 μg/l, this confirms the diagnosis of acromegaly.

stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. She has been given a diagnosis of Turner syndrome but has not attended medical follow up in the past because of parental wishes. Over the past three to six months she has developed progressively increasing shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. Her blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg,pulse is 72 bpm and regular. She has an aortic ejection systolic murmur. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her heart murmur?
explanation: The gradual fall off in exercise tolerance, coupled with an ejection systolic murmur,fits well with a diagnosis of bicuspid aortic valve, where valve disease has deteriorated to the point of clinically significant stenosis. Case series suggest that 18-30% of women with Turner syndrome have a diagnosis of bicuspid aortic valve.

stem: A56-year-old woman with a prolonged history of depression comes to the Emergency Department by paramedic ambulance. She was found by her daughter, delirious and suffering from a fever, that morning. Her daughter tells you she has recently commenced treatment for back pain and takes citalopram for her depression. She has a temperature of 38.9℃,her blood pressure is 149/89 mmHg. Her Glasgow Coma Scale(GCS) score is 13; you note bilateral increased tone, hyper-reflexia and spontaneous clonus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her presentation?
explanation: It is well established that tramadol has serotoninergic effects, which can precipitate presentation as here, with serotonin syndrome, manifest by pyrexia, confusion,increased muscle tone and hyper-reflexia. Withdrawal of the offending agents is the most important intervention, in this case both the citalopram and the tramadol should be discontinued. Supportive therapy for temperature,fluid balance and acid-base disturbance may also be required.

stem: A59-year-old retired tailor comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Over the past six to nine months, she has noticed increased pain and stiffness affecting the distal joints of the fingers of her right hand. Examination reveals evidence of distal interphalangeal(DIP) joint arthritis with Heberden's nodes. She finds no relief from regular paracetamol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: In this situation, with local finger osteoarthritis probably related to this patient's previous work as a tailor, topical NSAIDs are a reasonable next step after regular paracetamol. They may well control pain enough to allow her to regain some function in her fingers.

stem: A 45-year-old chef is referred to the Orthopaedic Clinic for review. He has pain in his hands at night and feels that he is dropping things in the kitchen. Examination reveals some wasting of the thenar eminence; sensation is diminished over the fingertips of the second and third digits. Where is the most likely site of injury in this patient?
explanation: The fact that sensation is preserved over the thenar eminence here is a strong pointer to distal median nerve injury, probably as a result of carpal tunnel syndrome. Provocative testing at the bedside to reproduce Tinel's sign or the Phalen test may reproduce symptoms of nocturnal paraesthesia.

stem: A72-year-old man who has ischaemic cardiovascular disease and two previous transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) comes to the Emergency Department with sudden deterioration of vision affecting his left eye. He says he awoke from sleep unable to do more than count fingers using his left eye and this has now deteriorated so that he can only perceive light and dark. Fundoscopy reveals a pale retina. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The sudden-onset loss of vision in a patient with a strong cardiovascular history and a pale retina on fundoscopy is suggestive of a central retinal artery occlusion. Treatment is directed at reducing intra-ocular pressure using agents such as acetazolamide, vasodilators or ocular massage. Aspirin is also usually also prescribed.

stem: A 29-year-old policeman comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has been bitten on the hand by a suspect. He washed the wound at the time and it was dressed at the police station. He is attending for further advice.You review the wound and can see a number of teeth marks with dried blood overlying the puncture wounds, with surrounding erythema. He is up to date with tetanus vaccination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Human bites normally lead to infection with a mixture of streptococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Eikenella corrodens and anaerobic bacteria. Co-amoxiclav is the preferred intervention for human bites and is recommended for all patients who present with an injury which is less than 72-hours old and for all bites where patients present later, with signs of infection.

stem: A52-year-old man with known alcoholism and oesophageal varices is admitted to the Emergency Department with a large upper gastrointestinal(GI) haemorrhage. He had defaulted from a previously planned endoscopy for banding some three months earlier. Medication of note includes B vitamins and propranolol, although it's not clear how much he complies with therapy. Examination reveals a BP of 85/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular.You note dried blood around his mouth and he is tender in the epigastrium. Intravenous(IV) fluid replacement is commenced. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 89 g/l 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 62×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 9.2 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/l International normalised ratio (INR) Which of the following is the most important next intervention?
explanation: National Institute for Clinical Excellence(NICE) guidelines are clear on the use of terlipressin in patients with suspected variceal haemorrhage, as here: Portal hypertension Media explanations 'Offer terlipressin to patients with suspected variceal bleeding at presentation. Stop treatment after definitive haemostasis has been achieved, or after five days, unless there is another indication for its use. Terlipressin has positive effects on portal blood flow,vasoconstricting dilated splanchnic blood vessels, and inducing changes in Gl smooth muscle which are also thought to reduce bleeding.

stem: A37-year-old carpenter comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has pain and swelling at the base of his thumb which is worse on pinching and grasping objects with the thumb and using his wrist. Examination confirms swelling and pain at the base of the thumb and the pain is worse when the wrist is deviated towards the ulnar side, with the thumb grasped in a closed fist. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pain and swelling?
options: Osteoarthritis at the base of the thumb
explanation: The pain and swelling at the base of the thumb, with worsening of symptoms on performing Finkelstein's test (ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb inside a clenched fist), are entirely consistent with a diagnosis of DQT.Although the aetiology of DQT is unknown, it may occur more commonly in individuals who have overuse of the thumb as sports people or in their job. Rest and splinting are the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. He was discharged from the hospital some four weeks earlier following right coronary artery stenting for an inferior myocardial infarction. His clopidogrel was stopped by the GP because of a per rectum (PR) bleed one week ago, although he has continued aspirin therapy. His blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 40 bpm and regular. He is pale and sweaty. Electrocardiogram(ECG) reveals 3 mm of ST elevation in II, II and atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Distal left anterior descending (LAD) artery occlusion
explanation: In-stent thrombosis occurs most commonly in the first 30 days after stent insertion. Re-endothelialisation occurs by month six, although dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended up to at least month 12 by the majority of guidelines. In this case, presentation with ST elevation in the same territory as the original myocardial infarction so soon after stopping clopidogrel means that in-stent thrombosis is the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A19-year-old man comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has emotional difficulty forming relationships and problems with his sexual function. Examination reveals a blood pressure(BP) of 110/80 mmHg, pulse is 68 bpm and regular. He is 184 cm in height and his body mass index(BMI) is 22 kg/m.He has bilateral gynaecomastia, sparse axillary and pubic hair and small testes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation: The phenotype described here fits with XXY chromosome type and a diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome. Supplementation with testosterone in this situation can significantly improve symptoms and prevent long- term complications of Klinefelter such as osteoporosis.

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by the police. He was found shouting in the street, believing that men who he has dealt drugs with are coming to kill him. He also believes that his parents are trying to give him medication against his will. According to his parents, he smokes strong cannabis every day and has never held down a job since leaving school. There are no abnormal physical findings, although you note he is unkempt and his clothes are dirty. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The heavy use of recreational cannabis, coupled with the paranoia displayed here, is consistent with cannabis-induced psychosis. Other features to suggest schizophrenia, such as thought insertion, thought broadcasting and primary delusional perception are absent here.

stem: A 44-year-old man is diagnosed with a left above-knee deep vein thrombosis (DVT). He is in good health, he takes no regular medications. General physical examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 139 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine transferase (ALT) 25 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 130 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 12 μmol/L 2-17μmol/L Chest X-ray unremarkable Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has an unprovoked DVT with no past medical history, an active lifestyle, normal physical examination and normal investigations.In this situation, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend checking baseline blood tests including PT(prothrombin time) and APTT (activated partial thromboplastin time). If all baseline blood tests are normal and there are no relevant clinical symtoms in cases of unprovoked DVT, further investigation is not required.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Haematology Clinic following an episode of prolonged bleeding following a wisdom tooth extraction. He tells you that his sister suffers from a similar problem, as does his father, and they have to take special care when undergoing minor surgical procedures. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 287×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/ Creatinine 72μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Prothrombin time (PT) 12s 10.6-14.9s Activated partial thromboplastin time(APTT) 35s 23.0-35.0 s Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The majority of VWD is inherited in autosomal-dominant fashion; this accounts for the fact that a number of members of the family are affected,including females, who have increased bleeding risk. APTT may be prolonged in 50% of patients with VWD because of co-existent reduced levels of factor VIII. Desmopressin may be given before procedures such as tooth extraction to reduce the risk of prolonged bleeding.

stem: A 23-year-old man is referred to the Cardiology Clinic by his GP with worsening exercise tolerance and increased shortness of breath over the past few months. The GP has noticed a diastolic murmur. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 122/80 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There is a soft diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge and you note mild pitting oedema of both ankles. The patient is 1.92 m tall and is thin, with a body mass index(BMI) of 19 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This young man is tall and thin, with a murmur consistent with pulmonary regurgitation. The suspicion is of underlying Marfan syndrome leading to dilatation of the pulmonary valve ring. The signs of early right-side heart failure also support this as the likely diagnosis.

stem: A 49-year-old hiker comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has just returned from a trip to Austria and has an area of erythema on his right lower leg. At the centre of it there is an eschar and he remembers a tick bite a few days earlier. He has no symptoms of neurological or cardiac dysfunction. He is apyrexial. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has symptoms consistent with erythema migrans related to a tick bite, raising the possibility that systemic symptoms of Lyme disease may follow.Three options for antibiotic intervention are recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE). Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is recommended for patients aged 12 and older. Where this is unsuitable or contraindicated, amoxicillin or azithromycin are potential alternatives.

stem: A 96-year-old woman with bilateral knee replacements comes to the clinic for review. She complains of urinary frequency, particularly at night, when she is occasionally unable to makeit to the toilet and is incontinent of urine. She takes antihypertensives but uses no other medication. Her blood pressure is 155/85 mmHg with a postural drop of 15mmHg on standing. Pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m. Routine bloods,including glucose, are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient is very elderly and likely to have significantly reduced mobility given her bilateral knee replacements. The easiest solution to her incontinence is a logistical one; placing a commode at the side of the bed which can be emptied in the morning should solve her problem of intermittent incontinence of urine.

stem: A 45-year-old man who suffered a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) some 14 days earlier which required placement of a coil has been readmitted to the Emergency Department with severe headaches and inability to look to the side. These symptoms are new, but he has some left face and arm weekness which hasn't changed since his orgiginal SAH. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 165/95 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular and he is apyrexial. Neurological examination reveals bilateral papilloedema, bilateral sixth nerve palsies and left face and arm weakness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Re-bleed from the original vascular lesion
explanation: The clues here include the severe headaches, coupled with neurological signs including papilloedema and sixth nerve palsies against a background of stable neurological deficit. Hydrocephalus is a common complication of SAH, documented by computed tomography(CT) scan in 40% of patients, 15% of whom are symptomatic.

stem: A70-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a pre-syncopal episode whilst at the local supermarket. She has gained 4 kg in weight over the past two months and feels like she is slowing down. She takes a number of medications for ischaemic heart disease. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg, her pulse is 40 bpm and regular. Body mass index(BMI) is 35 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Electrocardiogram(ECG) first-degree heart block,inferior Q waves Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Hypothyroidism Media explanations This patient's presentation with weight gain, pre-syncope, bradycardia and hyponatraemia fits well with a diagnosis of hypothyroidism, potentially due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis. The initial investigation of choice is TSH, which is likely to be markedly elevated.

stem: A37-year-old man comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He describes a history of a rash on both shins for around 3 months. He is otherwise well but does mention that he has lost some weight recently. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 125/82 mmHg,pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There is evidence of cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Auscultation of the chest revels no abnormalities. The rash on his shins is consistent with erythema nodosum. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 11.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Lymph node biopsy granuloma QuantiFERONR gamma test positive Tuberculin skin test negative Chest X-ray bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy Which of the following is the most likely cause of the positive QuantiFERON gamma test?
options: False positive due to eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis(EGPA)
explanation: the pattern of results here raises the possibility of latent TB. It's important to recognise here because the patient may well also have sarcoidosis, and if steroid therapy is considered, it may lead to reactivation of latent TB.

stem: A32-year-old woman who is a substance abuser, using nitrous oxide a number of times per week and drinking 50-60 units of alcohol, comes to the Emergency Department complaining of sudden visual loss affecting her right eye. Examination reveals an ataxic gait, bilateral loss of vibration sense and position, upgoing plantars and right optic disc pallor. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: The neurological features seen here with loss of joint position and vibration sense,upgoing plantars and optic neuritis, fit with B deficiency. The clue here apart from alcoholism, which may drive generalised B2 deficiency, is the presence of nitrous oxide abuse, which drives conversion of B2 from the active monovalent form to the inactive divalent form.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset severe lumbar spine pain and weakness of both lower limbs. The pain began some 24h earlier and has steadily worsened. She has a 60-pack-year smoking history and reports a chronic, worsening cough over the past six months. There is bilateral lower limb weakness(3/5) with increased tone and hyper-reflexia. Decreased anal sensation is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Conus medullaris syndrome is associated with lower limb weakness with increased tone, as is seen here. Hyper-reflexia is also noted. This is in contrast to a number of the other conditions listed which result in limb weakness with decreased tone. In this patient's case, a secondary tumour related to smoking is a possible cause.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following an overdose of digoxin. She is vomiting and complains of yellow vision. Her blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg, pulse is 40 bpm and regular. Which of the following is the primary mode of action of digoxin?
explanation: Digoxin inhibits the Na-K-ATPase membrane pump, resulting in an increase in intracellular sodium. In overdose, it is associated with nausea, vomiting and yellow discoloration of vision. The sodium calcium exchanger in turn increases in activity to pump out the sodium and in so doing, pumps in more calcium. The increase in intracellular calcium promotes an improvement in myocardial contractility and acting on the slope of phase IV depolarisation in cardiac myocytes.

stem: A 22-year-old student is brought to the Emergency Department by the police. His flatmates have become increasingly concerned about him over the past three months, as he has become increasingly withdrawn and is acting strangely. He told them he believes that his thoughts are being controlled by the radio and when he turns it on, he can hear voices providing a commentary on his actions. He refuses physical examination, is unkempt and has wrapped himself in tin foil to prevent transmission of his thoughts. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: Both Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network(SIGN) and the National Institute for Care and Health Excellence(NICE) guidelines recommend olanzapine or risperidone as initial options for the treatment of acute schizophrenia. In this situation, without significant agitation or aggression, benzodiazepines are potentially not required.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department some ten days after returning from a holiday in the West Indies. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse during his stay. He has a single ulcer over the glans penis and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: LV is endemic in India, the Caribbean, South America and south-east Asia. It is caused by infection with the L1,L2 or L3 serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis. The bacterium infects phagocytes, accounting for early presentation with a painless ulcer and rapid spread to lymph nodes, as is seen here. Doxycycline is the initial intervention.

stem: An 80-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has gross swelling and pain at the base of the right thumb and is unable to use her hand properly or flex her wrist.You confirm evidence of bony deformity, pain and limitation of movement. Her GP has been treating her with simple analgesia for osteoarthritis of the right hip. Apart from hypertension, she is otherwise well. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 454 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Corrected Calcium(Ca+) 2.40 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Phosphate(PO-) 1.0 mmol/L 0.70-1.40 mmol/L X-ray hand-bony deformity with destruction of the carporadial joint and new bone formation X-ray right hip-loss of joint space with joint destruction and new bone formation Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Although Paget's disease of the hand is only rarely described, it fits here with the destruction of a single joint, against a background of possible Paget's disease of the hip and pelvis and the raised ALP in the absence of other abnormal bone markers. There are no pointers in the past medical history to point to underlying malignancy.

stem: A 29-year-old drug abuser presents to the clinic for an infectious disease screening. She is concerned that she may have been infected with hepatitis B.Her antibody status is shown below: Hepatitis B surface antigen(HBsAg) positive Anti-hepatitis B core(HBc) positive Immunoglobulin M (IgM) anti-HBc positive Anti-hepatitis B surface antibody(HBs) negative Which of the following scenarios does that fit best with?
options: Immune due to natural hepatitis B infection
explanation: The presence of surface antigen, IgM anti-core antibodies, and anti-HBs negativity all imply acute hepatitis B infection. It's likely that injecting drug abuse is the cause.

stem: A74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department some two days after returning from a convention in Portugal. He began feeling unwell on the last day of his trip with a severe fever,joint and muscle pains. He has now developed a headache, dry cough with haemoptysis, severe shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. Diarrhoea has also begun around 12 hours earlier. His temperature is 39.6°℃,pulse is 95 bpm and regular, his blood pressure is 90/50.There is wheeze on auscultation, more marked at the left base. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 14.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 169×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 128 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 109μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein 289 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Chest X-ray left basal consolidation Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
explanation: This patient has Legionnaire's disease, as suggested by the onset of pneumonia in conjunction with a trip to a convention in southern Europe, the prodrome of flu-like symptoms, hyponatraemia and diarrhoea. Both quinolones and macrolides are effective in treating the condition, although modern quinolones such as levofloxacin may be associated with a reduction in morbidity.

stem: A 29-year-old professional rugby player presents to the Emergency Department after developing fast irregular palpitations while at a party to celebrate winning a challenge cup last night. He has no past medical history of note and has had a normal echocardiogram(ECHO) and exercise electrocardiogram(ECG) some six months earlier. His blood pressure is 115/80 mmHg, pulse is 135 bpm and irregular. His chest is clear and there is no ankle swelling. ECG reveals fast atrial fibrillation (AF). Chest X-ray(CXR) reveals a normal-sized heart. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Flecainide can be considered for chemical cardioversion in patients without structural heart disease who present with paroxysmal AF without structural heart disease, as here. Alcohol is often a precipitant for paroxysmal AFin previously healthy, fit individuals. An initial dose of 150 mg over 10-30 minutes is usually given intravenously(IV).

stem: A21-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with worsening peripheral oedema and headaches over the past few days. She is just recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection. She has suffered at least three previous episodes of peripheral oedema over the past four years, which each time responded to oral prednisolone. Her blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg, pulse is 72 bpm and regular.You confirm there is mild facial oedema and pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine dipstick protein ++ Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Glomerulonephritis(Nephrotic and Nephritic syndrome) Media explanations Where patients have responded previously to high-dose prednisolone against a background of minimal- change disease, they are likely to respond again. In this patient therefore, a trial of prednisolone is appropriate, with assessment of response at four to six weeks. In the event patients are hypertensive and/or the creatinine is elevated, angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibition is the intervention of choice for renoprotection.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has had type 1 diabetes for 50 years comes to the clinic for review. He has been diagnosed with proliferative diabetic retinopathy some five years ago, for which he received full scatter pan- retinal photocoagulation. What visual defect is he most likely to suffer from?
explanation: Full scatter pan-retinal photocoagulation is associated with reduced peripheral vision; reduced colour vision and impaired contrast sensitivity are also seen. Some of the peripheral field loss can be limited by moving to a mild scatter photocoagulation protocol.

stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. She has suffered from weight loss and increased anxiety over the past few months and reports palpitations at night. She is currently treated with sertraline and has been started on propranolol by her GP. Her blood pressure is 129/82 mmHg,pulse is 78 bpm and regular at rest and she has a fine tremor. You note smooth enlargement of the thyroid gland and mild tenderness. There is mild proptosis. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 289×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) 0.05μU/L 0.17-3.2μU/L Free T 8.2 pmol/L 3.5-5 pmol/L Free T 31 pmol/L 11-22 pmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The smooth thyroid enlargement coupled with signs, symptoms and biological confirmation of thyrotoxicosis, is consistent with a diagnosis of Graves'. Block replace with high-dose carbimazole and thyroxine replacement in combination is the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A35-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department having become unwell on a freighter which has just docked in port from Russia. He has been unwell with symptoms of a common cold for the past two days and now has a severe sore throat, such that he is unable to swallow, and nose bleeds. Examination reveals a pyrexia of 39℃, a pulse of 85 bpm and regular, and a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg.You note marked cervical lymphadenopathy,pharyngitis and a grey/white pseudomembrane overlying the inflamed pharyngeal tissue. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This man's symptoms are consistent with diphtheria, with the severe pharyngitis and pseudomembrane formation in a patient visiting from an area where there may not have been adequate vaccination coverage. A range of macrolides and penicillins are all appropriate in treating diphtheria,making azithromycin the most appropriate intervention.

stem: You are asked to review a 52-year-old man who has been admitted following a major upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. He has had a three units'blood transfusion and is continuing to bleed. He has ischaemic heart disease and has had an inferior myocardial infarction(MI) with stenting two years ago. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular. He is tender in the epigastrium. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 91 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2×109/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 62×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Prothrombin time(PT) 28.2 s 10.6-14.9s Activated partial thromboplastin time(APTT) 55.1s 23.0-35.0 s Fibrinogen 1.0 mg/l 1.25-3.00 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In this case, with active bleeding probably from a peptic ulcer, at least endoscopy and possibly laparotomy would be contemplated.Given the low fibrinogen (less than 1.5 g/L), the most appropriate next step according to National Institute for Clinical Excellence(NICE) guidelines is an adult dose of cryoprecipitate (two pools) with FFP.

stem: A 29-year-old carpenter comes to the clinic for review.He injured his hand when it was crushed by a pile of wood and feels there is some residual weakness of his thumb. Neurological examination demonstrates weakness of flexion of the terminal phalanx of the thumb.
explanation: This patient has weakness of flexor pollicis longus, which is supplied by a branch of the median nerve. The median nerve supplies the flexor and pronator muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm(except the flexor carpi ulnaris and part of the flexor digitorum profundus,innervated by the ulnar nerve). The nerve also provides motor supply to the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals in the hand.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and a previous inferior myocardial infarction comes to the Emergency Department. He has suffered two episodes of loss of vision affecting his left eye in the last two weeks that he describes as like a curtain coming down, the latest episode on the morning of admission. By the time you see him in the department, his vision has recovered and fundoscopy is unremarkable. Blood pressure is raised at 155/94 mmHg. Pulse is 72 bpm and regular. Where is the likely source of the embolus which has caused his symptoms?
explanation: This patient reports an episode of amaurosis fugax, which is due to transient occlusion of the ophthalmic or retinal artery, and often arises as a result of an embolism from atheroma within the ipsilateral internal carotid artery. Carotid duplex scanning is therefore essential as part of urgent work-up of this case.

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and fast atrial fibrillation. She is currently being treated with trastuzumab for a breast cancer. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 125 bpm and atrial fibrillation (AF). There are crackles at both lung bases on auscultation. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of trastuzumab?
options: Human epidermal growth factor receptor(HER)1 agonist
explanation: Trastuzumab is a recombinant humanised immunoglobulin G1(IgG1)monoclonal antibody against HER2. HER2 is over-expressed in 20-30% of primary breast cancers, and patients with tumours which over- express HER2 have a shortened disease-free survival and life expectancy. Trastuzumab has a response rate superior to taxanes when used as monotherapy, which is improved further when the drug is used in combination with taxanes (around 49% vs 34% for docetaxel alone in metastatic breast cancer). HER2 antagonism is also a cause of cardiomyopathy, accountable for the presentation with AF seen here.

stem: A 23-year-old man with ulcerative colitis (UC) comes to the clinic for review. He is taking regular oral mesalazine and a course of oral prednisolone, but despite this, is continuing to open his bowels four times per day and has some left-sided abdominal pain that has increased over the past three months.You confirm mild left iliac fossa tenderness on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 352×10/ 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 49 mg/l 0-10 mg/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 89 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term intervention for his UC?
explanation: Ulcerative colitis Media explanations Azathioprine is the disease-modifying agent of choice for the treatment of UC. It is indicated when patients require two or more corticosteroid courses in a calendar year, have disease relapses when steroid dose goes below 15mg/day, or a relapse occurs within six weeks of stopping a steroid course.

stem: A72-year-old woman was admitted with symptoms of meningitis. She has recently returned from a holiday in northern France with her husband. She has had a persistent headache with worsening neck stiffness over the past few days. The admitting team were unable to perform a lumbar puncture and started empirical ceftriaxone. You are asked to review her because her symptoms have not improved. A lumbar puncture shows Gram-positive bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her meningitis?
explanation: Listeria meningitis is commoner in the elderly and in pregnant women,and the source of infection in this case may have been unpasteurised cheese. The infection does not respond to ceftriaxone, which explains why there has been no improvement despite intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy.Ampicillin and gentamicin are more appropriate potential interventions.

stem: A 49-year-old man who has increased in weight by 8kg over the past three months is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with a raised 24-hour urinary free cortisol. He also has impaired glucose tolerance, and hypertension which has worsened over the past few months. His body mass index(BMI) is 36 kg/m.Bloods reveal a metabolic alkalosis. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Urinary cortisol testing does carry a false-positive rate, confirmatory testing is therefore required, with dexamethasone-suppression testing an appropriate next step.1mg of dexamethasone is ingested at 2300, and cortisol is measured at 0800 the following morning. Where cortisol fails to suppress, Cushing syndrome is suggested.

stem: A73-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe diarrhoea containing blood and mucus. She has been suffering from increasing abdominal cramps and lower gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms for the past three days. Five days ago, she attended a wedding party. Her temperature is 38.6°℃, blood pressure(BP) is 95/60 mmHg and pulse is 93 bpm. The abdomen is soft,although there is general tenderness with active bowel sounds. Intravenous (IV) fluids are commenced. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 15.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 402×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 189 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 12.2 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The features here are suggestive of campylobacter infection, which occurs due to ingestion of contaminated meat or dairy products, the wedding meal likely to have been the source of infection. The low BP,elevated creatinine and urea all imply significant symptoms, meaning antibiotics are indicated. Macrolides including azithromycin or erythromycin are potential treatment options.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Pharmacology Clinic for review of her blood pressure management. She is taking a combination of amlodipine and indapamide but is still hypertensive with a clinic blood pressure of 155/95 mmHg. Her pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22kg/m.Creatinine is elevated at 120 μmol/L, potassium is 3.4 mmol/l and ultrasound reveals asymmetrical kidneys with a shrunken kidney on the left-hand side. Urine is dipstick positive for protein. Which of the following is the most likely cause of hypertension in this patient?
explanation: The age of this patient and the differential kidney size on ultrasound scanning raises the possibility of unilateral renal-artery stenosis.Duplex ultrasonography may indicate impaired flow through the renal artery on the affected side, although computed tomography(CT) angiography is a more definitive investigation to confirm the diagnosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE) comes to the clinic for review. She is currently well controlled on hydroxychloroquine. Which of the following markers would be best to assess disease activity in this patient?
explanation: Antibody titres may increase with increased lupus activity, stay the same, or even decrease in some cases. In contrast, tissue inflammation leads to increased consumption of complement factors, C3 in particular.The most useful laboratory tests to predict an SLE flare(diease activity) are the onset of an increased serum titer of anti-dsDNA antibodies and a fall in complement levels (especially CH50,C3, and C4). Persistently low serum levels of complement C1q are also associated with activity of lupus nephritis.Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) and full blood count may also be helpful.

stem: A38-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. Over the past year, there has been a gradual increase in his alkaline phosphatase and transaminases. He takes regular mesalazine for control of his ulcerative colitis (UC) but is otherwise well. You suspect he may be developing primary sclerosing cholangitis(PSC). Which of the following is the optimal investigation to diagnose PSC?
explanation: PSC is a chronic cholestatic disorder characterised by inflammation and fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, resulting in multifocal biliary strictures. MRCP is non-invasive and is excellent at demonstrating bile duct structures with both duct dilatation and stenosis. It is therefore the optimal investigation here.

stem: A75-year-old man is admitted with sudden-onset vomiting, vertigo and double vision. He has a medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes and takes multiple medications. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular.You note right-sided Horner syndrome, facial weakness and sensory loss. There is left-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation affecting the torso and limbs. What is the cause of his presentation?
explanation: This patient presents with features of lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. This causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome,facial sensory loss, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation. It occurs because of ischaemia affecting the lateral portion of the medulla oblongata in the brainstem.

stem: A41-year-old woman who works as a care assistant in a nursing home comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has an intensely itchy papular rash which has developed over the pasttwo to three weeks. She particularly feels the urge to scratch her hands, where the web spaces are between her fingers. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient most likely has scabies, transferred from a resident in the nursing home. Permethrin 5% dermal cream is the most widely studied agent for the treatment of scabies. It has been shown more effective than topical crotamiton and oral ivermectin. In patients with Norwegian scabies, repeated application of permethrin on two or three consecutive days may be required.

stem: A72-year-old woman is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic with primary hyperparathyroidism. Her GP has noted that she has a phosphate below the lower limit of the normal range (0.6 mmol/L) and an elevated calcium of 2.9 mmol/L. Where is the most pronounced effect of parathyroid hormone(PTH) on phosphate reabsorption?
options: Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Descending limb of loop of Henle
explanation: Around 85% of phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by the sodium/phosphate cotransporter. Its action is inhibited by PTH, leading to increased phosphate excretion.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is reviewed some 14 days post-renal transplant from a cytomegalovirus(CMV)- positive donor. She has been treated with CMV prophylaxis and a tacrolimus- and prednisolone-based immunosuppressive regimen. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 142/88 mmHg,and pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There is erythema over her scar and minor tenderness over the transplanted kidney. Estimated glomerular filtration rate(eGFR) has fallen by 30 ml/min since immediately post-transplant. C-reactive protein test (CRP) is 29 mg/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute rejection can occur for up to six months after renal transplantation and as here, may be associated with a decrease in eGFR in the absence of other symptoms. Radiographic imaging is generally performed to rule out other causes of renal impairment, donor-derived deoxyribonucleic acid(DNA) can be measured in serum to look for breakdown of the graft, although biopsy of the graft is the gold standard to determine the nature of any rejection and guide appropriate intervention.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is managed with basal-bolus insulin therapy. His renal function has steadily worsened over the past 18 months, and his GP is finding it increasingly difficult to manage his blood pressure. Current medication includes ramipril 10 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg and amlodipine 5mg. His blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular. There is pitting oedema of both lower limbs. His body mass index is 32 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 302 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine albumin:creatinine ratio 510 mg/mmol 30-300 mg/mmol HbA 1c(glycosylated Hb) 48 mmol/mol 53 mmol/mol Which of the following is the most likely cause of his renal impairment?
explanation: Although this patient's HbA1c is now well controlled, he has suffered from type 2 diabetes for 15 years, implying significant exposure to elevated blood glucose levels. This, coupled with obesity and hypertension, has undoubtedly driven this patient's hypertension with marked proteinuria. Tight control of blood pressure, including continuing angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibition is crucial in slowing further deterioration in renal function.

stem: A 35-year-old man who has suffered from ankylosing spondylitis for many years comes to the clinic for review. He now suffers from shortness of breath after walking only a short distance. He is a non-smoker. Examination reveals significantly reduced forward and lateral flexion of the spine and evidence of limited chest expansion. There are quiet breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrates evidence of apical fibrosis. Which of the following is most likely to be found on pulmonary function testing?
options: Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC)70%
Increased diffusing capacity of the lung(DLCO)
Reduced KCO (coefficient of carbon monoxide transfer)
explanation: With changes seen on CT scanning consistent with ankylosing spondylitis, it's likely that diffusion of carbon monoxide would be reduced, in keeping with clinically significant pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man who is known to be human immunodeficiency virus(HIV) positive comes to the clinic for review. He has developed a rash affecting his thighs, buttocks, groin and lower abdomen. On examination, you can see a number of clusters of firm, flesh colored, umbilicated papules, most around 5mm, but some much larger in diameter. Which of the following viruses is the most likely cause of the skin lesions?
explanation: MCV-1 is the commonest cause of molluscum contagiosum, the cause of the skin changes seen here. MCV-2 is also seen, particularly in patients with HIV infection; although in patients not infected with HIV, lesions are usually between 1 mm and 5 mm,in those who are HIV positive they may approach 1 cm or greater in diameter.

stem: A55-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has a previous abdominal hysterectomy and has been suffering from stress incontinence for the past six months. Despite pelvic floor exercises, she is still suffering one or more accidents with urinary incontinence each day. Her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. She refuses further surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: NICE advises that duloxetine may be conisdered as a second-line option for the treatment of stress incontinence (pelvic floor muscle training and then progression to surgical intervention is the default path). It may be considered for patients who refuse surgical intervention or is not suitable for surgical treatment.In urinary incontinence, duloxetine is thought to increase activity of the urethral sphincter.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic for review. She has suffered from intermittent episodes of haematuria, associated with upper respiratory tract infection, over the past three years. These have resolved spontaneously. She now presents with a sore throat of three days' duration and has haematuria once again. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. She has reddening over her tonsils. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×109/ 4-11×10/L Platelets 302×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 89μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine blood +, protein negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient almost certainly has immunoglobulin A(lgA) nephropathy at low risk of progression to chronic renal impairment, given her normal blood pressure and haematuria in the absence of proteinuria. As such, monitoring of blood pressure, urine analysis and creatinine is the most appropriate next step.

stem: A 64-year-old man with chronic renal impairment as a result of type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He has been feeling increasingly tired over the past few months and has trouble climbing the stairs because of pains around his hips and thighs. He takes a number of medications including ramipril, indapamide, and a basal-bolus insulin regimen. His blood pressure is 152/84 mmHg,pulse is 68 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 32 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 95 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 289 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Phosphate(PO-) 1.8 mmol/L 0.70-1.40 mmol/L Glucose 8.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Corrected Ca+ 2.1 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 212 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Albumin 34 g/L 35-55 g/L parathyroid hormone (PTH) 14.2 pmol/l 1.6-6.9 pmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has chronic kidney disease with evidence of borderline hypocalcaemia, phosphate retention, an elevated alkaline phosphatase and elevated PTH.The PTH is more than twice the upper limit of normal, treatment is therefore indicated with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. He should also follow a low- phosphate diet.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has benign prostatic hypertrophy comes to the Emergency Department with nausea and anorexia which has progressively worsened over the last few days. He is unable to pass urine and has abdominal discomfort. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He has lower abdominal pain on palpation. A bladder scan reveals approximately 700 ml within the bladder. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 7.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 391μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 17 mmol/l 24-30 mmol/L Calcium gluconate, insulin and dextrose, and separate intravenous (IV) normal saline fluid replacement are Which of the following is the most important next step? commenced.
explanation: This patient has post-renal failure, which is almost certainly recoverable. Catheterisation is the next intervention of choice, whilst ensuring that fluid replacement, usually by a combination of oral and IV routes, is adequate to replace losses.

stem: A59-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review to discuss why she has suffered a second episode of cholecystitis in the last year. She is interested in the constituents of gallbladder bile. Which of the following is the largest constituent of bile?
explanation: Somewhat unsurprisingly, bile salts make up the largest component of bile, at around 60 g/L.Two primary amino acids are produced by the liver, cholic acid is the most abundant bile acid, chenodeoxycholic acid is also produced. They are conjugated with two amino acids to form eight possible bile salts.

stem: A32-year-old man of Chinese origin comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has recently been started on carbamazepine for complex partial epilepsy and is suffering from a severe skin rash. Examination reveals extensive annular lesions, a number of which have blistered. There is extensive cracking and blistering of the lips and a number of ulcers in the mouth. He has a temperature of 38.2℃, his pulse is 92 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Human leukocyte antigen(HLA) B1502 is associated with the development of SJS in patients prescribed carbamazepine. SJS is suggested by the extensive erythema multiforme-type rash with blistering, particularly when it affects mucus membranes. Discontinuation of the causative medication, coupled with adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement and pain relief are the main pillars of intervention.

stem: An 18-year-old man is reviewed in the clinic with deteriorating colour and night vision and appears to be suffering from maculopathy. Other members of the family are similarly affected, and it is thought he is suffering from an inherited peroxisome disorder. Which of the following correctly describes peroxisome function?
options: Oxidation of branched chain fatty acids (BCFAs)
explanation: The primary function of peroxisomes is to oxidise BCFAs to liberate energy. Refsum's disease, the potential diagnosis here, occurs because of impaired beta-oxidation of BCFAs, which leads to a build-up of phytanic acid and its derivatives in plasma and tissues. It leads to progressive visual loss with impaired night and colour vision which progresses over time.
